title: Module 5: Controlling Access
description: Application/menu/module visibility, Access Control rules (table.None / table.field / table.* and evaluation order), the four ACL permission checks, ACL scripting and debugging, application (cross-scope) access, web service access, caller access, and protection policies.

questions.prompt: What is ServiceNow's default access posture, and what does it imply for new tables?

choices.text: Allow by default, so ACLs are only ever needed in order to restrict access.
Deny by default, so an ACL must grant access or it is refused.
Allow for admins only, while all other access must be explicitly scripted.
Access is determined solely by the roles set on the application menu itself.

questions.explanation: ServiceNow denies access by default; an ACL must grant it. This is why four basic CRUD ACLs are generated automatically when a table is created with a role.

questions.prompt: An application menu's Roles field is left empty. Who can see that menu?

choices.text: No one until a role is added.
Only admins.
Everyone.
Only users who can see at least one of its modules.

questions.explanation: An application menu with no role listed is visible to everyone (this is how the Self-Service menu works). If roles are listed, a user needs at least one of them.

questions.prompt: A module record has its Roles field left blank. What determines whether a user sees the module?

choices.text: Everyone sees it, regardless of whether they can see the parent application menu.
It is visible to anyone who can see its parent application menu.
Only admins see it.
No one is able to see the module at all until a qualifying role is explicitly added to it.

questions.explanation: For a module, a blank Roles field does not mean everyone. It means the module is visible to anyone who can see its parent application menu. You can also require a different/additional role on the module.

questions.prompt: Why is hiding application menus and modules considered convenience rather than true security?

choices.text: Because application menus and modules cannot have any roles assigned to them at all.
Because a user can still reach records directly, e.g. via a direct link or table_name.list.
Because the roles set on menus are completely ignored by the platform at runtime anyway.
Because only admins can see the navigator.

questions.explanation: Navigation visibility only hides the UI link. A user can still reach records via a direct link or by typing <table>.list. Actual data access is governed by Access Control rules, not menu/module visibility.

questions.prompt: What role must a user elevate to in order to create or edit Access Control rules?

choices.text: admin
security_admin
view_changer
itil_admin

questions.explanation: Editing/creating ACLs requires elevating to the security_admin role from the user menu. Not all admins have this elevated role, and if Studio still blocks you after elevating, saving any application file refreshes its permissions.

questions.prompt: Which ACL type controls access at the row/record level and must be passed before any field can be accessed?

choices.text: table.field
table.*
table.None

questions.explanation: A table.None rule governs the table's rows. You must pass it to see the table's list/forms at all; if the table-level check is denied, no field-level rule can grant access.

questions.prompt: What does a table.* (wildcard) ACL apply to?

choices.text: Every field on the record where there is no field-specific ACL.
Only the record's row-level access.
Every table in the application scope.
Only those fields that already have their own field-specific ACL defined on them.

questions.explanation: A table.* rule applies to every field on the record where no field-specific (table.field) ACL exists. A more specific field rule overrides the wildcard.

questions.prompt: When two ACLs could both apply to a field, which one wins?

choices.text: The more general wildcard rule (table.*) always overrides the specific field rule.
The more specific rule (table.field) overrides the general one (table.*).
Whichever of the two rules happens to have the lower Order value number wins out here.
The two rules are simply combined together using AND logic at evaluation time.

questions.explanation: The more specific rule wins. A field-specific table.field rule overrides a general table.* wildcard rule, similar to CSS specificity.

questions.prompt: How does introducing a table.* ACL change the default assumption about field visibility?

choices.text: It makes every field on the record visible to all users, regardless of their role or any ACLs.
It flips the default: fields are locked unless the user matches table.* or a specific field ACL.
It disables all field-specific rules.
It only affects the row-level (table.None) check.

questions.explanation: Without a table.* rule, users are assumed to have access to all fields unless a field rule excludes them (easy to include). Adding table.* flips it: everything is locked unless the user matches the wildcard role or a specific field ACL grants access (easy to exclude/cherry-pick).

questions.prompt: Goal: 'asset' sees all fields, 'catalog' sees ONLY field 3. You have table.None (asset, catalog), table.* Read for asset, and table.field_3 Read for catalog only. What is the result, and the fix?

choices.text: It works as intended; no change needed.
It fails: asset loses field 3 because the specific field rule overrides asset's wildcard. Fix: add asset to the table.field_3 rule.
It fails: catalog ends up seeing nothing at all because the wildcard blocks it. Fix: remove the table.* Read rule entirely.
It fails: both lose access. Fix: delete the table.None rule.

questions.explanation: The table.field_3 rule (catalog only) is more specific than asset's table.*, so it overrides it and asset loses field 3. Adding asset to the table.field_3 rule restores asset's full access while keeping catalog limited to field 3.

questions.prompt: In what order are Access Control rules evaluated for a record object?

choices.text: Field-level rules are always evaluated first, then table-level rules, each ordered from most specific to most general.
Table-level rules first (most specific to most general), then field-level rules (most specific to most general).
All rules at once, lowest Order wins.
Script rules first, then role rules.

questions.explanation: The system checks table-level rules first, most specific to most general, then field-level rules, most specific to most general. You must pass both a table rule and a field rule to access a record object.

questions.prompt: A user passes the table.None rule but fails the relevant field ACL. What happens?

choices.text: They are denied access to the entire table and all of the records in it.
They can access the record but not that particular field.
The field rule is ignored entirely because the table-level rule already passed for them.
They get full access because table rules take priority.

questions.explanation: Passing the table rule but failing a field rule means the user can interact with the record but cannot access the field described by that field ACL. Failing the table rule, by contrast, denies all fields.

questions.prompt: A single Access Control rule grants access only if all of its checks pass. Which checks are evaluated? (Choose 3)

choices.text: Role (user has one of the listed roles, or the list is empty).
Condition / data condition (Condition Builder evaluates true, or empty).
Script (advanced script returns true / sets answer to true, or empty).
The user's email domain matches the instance domain.

questions.explanation: An ACL has four checks evaluated in order, all of which must be true: Role, Security attribute, Condition (data condition), and Script. Email domain is not one of them.

questions.prompt: Within a single ACL you specify a role, a data condition, and a script. What must be true for the user to pass?

choices.text: Any one of the three checks passes.
All three checks pass (AND logic).
Only the role check matters; the rest are advisory.
The script overrides the role and condition.

questions.explanation: Within one ACL, all specified checks must evaluate true (AND). Adding more conditions to a single ACL makes it more specific and harder to pass.

questions.prompt: There are several separate read ACLs for the same table and operation (for example incident.None read). What does having multiple such ACLs mean?

choices.text: Access is more locked down, because the user is now required to pass every single one of these ACLs to get in.
Each ACL is a separate case; passing any one grants access (like multiple keys for one lock).
Only the single most recently created ACL for that operation is ever actually evaluated at runtime.
The ACLs cancel each other out.

questions.explanation: Multiple ACLs for the same operation each represent a separate context in which a user might pass (OR logic). More ACLs means more ways to be granted access, not a tighter lock. This is contextual security.

questions.prompt: When a table is created and the four basic CRUD ACLs are generated, how is the create permission defined by default?

choices.text: Create always requires the admin role specifically, no matter how the other CRUD ACLs are set up.
Create reuses the write (update) permissions unless you define an explicit create ACL.
By default, the create operation is denied to absolutely everyone until it is configured.
Create reuses the read permissions.

questions.explanation: The wildcard create ACL reuses the write permissions, so create permission equals write permission unless an explicit create-operation ACL is defined.

questions.prompt: Which methods are appropriate inside server-side Access Control scripts? (Choose 2)

choices.text: gs.hasRole()
current.isNewRecord()
g_form.getValue()
g_user.hasRole()

questions.explanation: ACL scripts run server-side, so GlideSystem (gs.hasRole) and GlideRecord (current.isNewRecord) are valid. g_form and g_user are client-side and unavailable. Also avoid GlideRecord queries in ACL scripts for performance.

questions.prompt: Why is client-side configuration (such as g_user.hasRole() or hiding a field with a UI policy) unacceptable as a security control?

choices.text: Client-side scripts cannot read user roles at all, so any such security check is meaningless from the very start.
The data is still sent to the browser and visible in the XML/page source, so hiding it is cosmetic only.
UI policies only run for admins.
g_user is not available on the client.

questions.explanation: Client-side hiding only reduces form clutter; the server still sends the data, which remains visible in the XML/page source. Security must be enforced server-side via ACLs and GlideSystem methods.

questions.prompt: Where do you enable ACL debugging that shows which rules apply to each field and whether they passed?

choices.text: System Security > Debugging > Debug Security Rules
System Definition > Tables, then open the Columns related list there
System UI > Forms
System Properties > Security

questions.explanation: Debug Security Rules (under System Security > Debugging) adds a bug icon beside each field and an ACL dump at the bottom of pages. Stop via Stop Debugging.

questions.prompt: In the color-coded ACL debug output, what does a gray entry indicate?

choices.text: The rule passed and explicitly granted the user read access to that particular field here.
The rule failed, so the user was explicitly denied access to that particular field outright.
The rule was skipped because a higher rule in the hierarchy already decided access.
The result came from cache.

questions.explanation: Gray = skipped because of an Access Control higher in the hierarchy. Green/blue check = passed, red X = failed, blue = previously cached result. Evaluation order shown is roles, security attribute, condition, script.

questions.prompt: What is the relationship between application access and Access Control rules?

choices.text: Application access completely replaces ACLs for scoped applications across the board.
Application access is evaluated in addition to ACLs and is configured per table.
Application access only applies to the UI layer, never to any server-side scripts or queries.
ACLs only apply when application access is set to None.

questions.explanation: Application access is evaluated in addition to ACLs and is configured on a table-by-table basis via the Application Access tab. It governs cross-scope CRUD, web service, and script access.

questions.prompt: Application access controls cross-scope access. To which scripts does it NOT apply?

choices.text: Scripts running in the same scope as the table.
Scripts running in the global (cross-scope) application scope on the instance.
Business rules on the table.
Any server-side script.

questions.explanation: Application access applies to all server-side scripts but does not apply to scripts executing in the same scope as the table. An app can always reach its own tables.

questions.prompt: When a table's Accessible from is set to All application scopes, what is the default level of cross-scope access?

choices.text: Full CRUD.
Read access only.
No access until explicitly granted.
Create and read only.

questions.explanation: Granting access to All application scopes defaults to read-only; create, update, and delete must be explicitly enabled.

questions.prompt: A global-scope script runs a GlideRecord update against a table whose application access allows read but not update from other scopes. What happens?

choices.text: A runtime error halts the script.
The update is silently allowed at runtime because GlideRecord operations completely bypass application access.
The unauthorized update is skipped, no error is thrown, and ServiceNow keeps running with a log message.
The whole table is locked for all scopes.

questions.explanation: Unauthorized cross-scope access is prevented at runtime without throwing an error: the offending operation is skipped and ServiceNow keeps running, logging a message like 'Security restricted: Write operation ... refused due to the table's cross-scope access policy.'

questions.prompt: A user record is flagged 'Web service access only'. What does this restrict?

choices.text: The user can never be added to any groups, roles, or teams anywhere in the entire instance configuration at all.
The user cannot log into the ServiceNow UI; the credentials authenticate web service/integration requests only.
The user bypasses all ACLs.
The user can only read data, never write.

questions.explanation: Web service access only prevents interactive UI login; the credentials authenticate web service/integration requests. The user is otherwise normal (groups, roles) and is still subject to ACL security.

questions.prompt: What does the 'Allow configuration' option enable?

choices.text: Other scopes to create artifacts (Dictionary Entries, UI Actions, Client Scripts) on your table.
End users to reconfigure forms, lists, and related lists at runtime without any developer involvement.
The automatic creation of all four CRUD ACLs whenever the table is first created in Studio.
Cross-instance publishing of the application.

questions.explanation: Allow configuration permits other scopes to create artifacts (Dictionary Entry, UI Action, Client Script, and other metadata) for your table, for example owning a button on an out-of-scope table. It is only selectable when Accessible from is All application scopes.

questions.prompt: With Caller Tracking, what happens when an out-of-scope caller accesses your resource?

choices.text: The cross-scope call is denied outright and stays blocked until an administrator manually approves it later.
The call is auto-approved and a record is created in the Restricted Caller Access table with status Allowed.
Nothing is recorded; access depends only on Accessible from.
The caller's scope is permanently blocked.

questions.explanation: Caller Tracking auto-approves the call and records it in the Restricted Caller Access table with status Allowed (an ask-forgiveness paper trail). Caller Restriction instead creates the record as Requested and requires manual approval.

questions.prompt: Which Caller Access setting requires that each cross-scope request be manually approved?

choices.text: --None--
Caller Tracking
Caller Restriction
Caller Logging

questions.explanation: Caller Restriction tracks each request with status Requested and requires manual approval (ask-permission). Caller Tracking auto-approves; --None-- defers to the Accessible from value.

questions.prompt: Under which circumstances do protection policies actually take effect?

choices.text: On the development instance itself, to hide an artifact's scripts from other developers on the team.
When the app is distributed via an update set.
When the app is installed from the ServiceNow Store or migrated from the Application Repository.
Whenever a UI policy hides the field.

questions.explanation: Protection policies apply only when an app is installed from the ServiceNow Store or migrated from the Application Repository. They are not applied via update set and do not affect the development instance, where you use ACLs/roles to restrict artifact access.

questions.prompt: Which protection policy value makes an artifact's logic completely non-viewable (a black box)?

choices.text: --None--
Read-only
Protected
Hidden

questions.explanation: Protected = logic is not viewable. Read-only = viewable but not editable. --None-- = viewable and editable. Protection policies apply to artifacts such as UI Actions and Script Includes.

questions.prompt: A single access control rule matches an operation a user is attempting. Which requirements must ALL be satisfied before that rule grants the operation? (Choose 3.)

choices.text: The condition defined on the access control evaluates to true.
The script defined on the access control evaluates to true, or sets the answer variable to true.
The user holds at least one role from the rule's required roles list, or that list is empty.
At least one other matching access control on the same table also evaluates to true.

questions.explanation: A matching rule grants access only when its condition is true, its script is true (or sets answer to true), and the user has one of the required roles (an empty role list passes automatically). The requirement about another rule on the same table is wrong: when several rules match at the same level, they are OR'd, so only one needs to pass. The AND relationship applies across levels instead, where the matching table-level and field-level rules must both succeed for a field operation.

questions.prompt: Which records track cross-scope applications and scripts that request access to a resource in another application scope?

choices.text: Restricted Caller Access records
Caller Tracking records
Cross-scope Access records
Access Control records

questions.explanation: Cross-scope access requests are stored in the Restricted Caller Access table (sys_restricted_caller_access). Caller Tracking is a value of the Caller Access field, not a separate record type. Cross-scope Access is not a table, and Access Controls govern user permissions on records, not cross-scope script calls.

questions.prompt: On an application resource, what is the difference between setting the Caller Access field to Caller Tracking versus Caller Restriction?

choices.text: Caller Tracking auto-approves cross-scope calls and logs them as Allowed; Caller Restriction denies calls until they are manually approved (logged as Requested).
Caller Tracking blocks all cross-scope calls; Caller Restriction allows all cross-scope calls automatically.
Both block cross-scope calls; they differ only in whether an email notification is sent to the resource owner.
Caller Tracking applies only to REST calls, while Caller Restriction applies only to script calls.

questions.explanation: Caller Tracking automatically approves cross-scope calls and records them in the Restricted Caller Access table with a status of Allowed, giving visibility without friction. Caller Restriction denies calls by default and requires manual approval, recording them with a status of Requested until granted. The None option instead defers entirely to the resource's Accessible from setting.
